title: How Much Does a Lawyer Cost? Fee Types, Rates and Worked Examples (2026)
description: What lawyers charge in 2026: the $349 average hourly rate, flat fees, retainers and contingency fees, plus court fees billed separately.
h1: How much does a lawyer cost?
summary: Clio's 2025 Legal Trends data puts the average U.S. lawyer hourly rate at $349, but your total depends on how the lawyer bills: hourly against a retainer, a flat fee for a defined task, or a contingency percentage of any recovery. Government fees are separate from the lawyer's fee, for example $405 to file a federal civil lawsuit or $338 to file a Chapter 7 bankruptcy. The only reliable figure for your matter is a written fee quote that states the scope of the work.
body:
What the headline numbers actually mean

The most widely quoted benchmark is Clio's national average hourly rate for lawyers: $349 per hour in its 2025 Legal Trends data[1]. That is an average across practice areas and states, so a quote you receive may sit well above or below it. Treat it as a reference point for checking arithmetic, not as a price list.

You will also see government wage figures. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median lawyer pay of $159,670 a year, or $76.76 an hour, for May 2025[2]. That is what lawyers earn, not what clients pay. A billing rate has to cover the lawyer's salary plus staff, rent, insurance, software and the hours that cannot be billed, which is why billing rates are several times the wage figure.

The four ways lawyers charge

Common fee arrangements and what to check in each
ArrangementWhat you payWhere you usually see itWhat to check
HourlyRate × time actually spent, often drawn from a depositDisputes, litigation, advice on changing factsRate for each person who works on the file; billing increment; monthly invoices
Flat feeOne price for a defined taskSimple wills, uncontested filings, document drafting, some criminal and immigration workExactly what is included and what triggers extra charges
ContingencyA percentage of the money recovered; no fee if nothing is recoveredPersonal injury, some employment and consumer claimsPercentage at each stage; whether costs come out before or after the fee
Retainer (advance deposit)Money paid up front and billed againstMost hourly mattersWhether unused funds are refunded and when the deposit must be topped up

Under ABA Model Rule 1.5, which most states have adopted in some form, a lawyer must tell you the scope of the work and the basis or rate of the fee, preferably in writing, before or soon after the work starts. Contingency agreements must be in a writing signed by the client, and contingency fees are barred in criminal defense and in divorce matters where the fee would depend on securing the divorce or on the amount of support or property awarded[3]. Money you pay in advance belongs in a client trust account until the lawyer earns it[4].

For a deeper comparison see hourly vs. flat fee and how contingency fees work.

Three worked examples

These examples use Clio's $349 national average[1] only to show the arithmetic. They are not quotes and not typical prices for any practice area.

Example 1: a one-off contract review. A lawyer estimates 3 hours to review a lease and explain the risks. 3 hours × $349 = $1,047. If the same lawyer offered a flat fee of $900, the flat fee would be cheaper unless the review took less than about 2.6 hours ($900 ÷ $349 = 2.58 hours).

Example 2: a contested civil case in California. Suppose the case needs 40 hours of lawyer time before it settles. 40 × $349 = $13,960 in fees. Filing the complaint as an unlimited civil case (over $35,000) adds a $435 first-paper fee[5]. Total before other costs: $13,960 + $435 = $14,395. Depositions, experts and service of process would be extra; see how much a lawsuit costs.

Example 3: a contingency case. A client agrees to a one-third fee and the claim settles for $60,000. $60,000 × 1/3 = $20,000 to the lawyer, before case costs. The percentage here is only an assumption for the arithmetic; percentages are set by agreement and some laws cap them.

Fees that are not the lawyer's

Many legal matters carry fixed government fees on top of anything a lawyer charges. Ask every lawyer whether their quote includes them.

Examples of official fees and fee limits (checked October 2026)
MatterOfficial fee or limitRelated guide
New civil lawsuit in federal district court$405 ($350 statutory fee + $55 administrative fee)[6][7]Lawsuit cost
Chapter 7 / Chapter 13 bankruptcy$338 / $313[8]Bankruptcy lawyer cost
Federal trademark application$350 per class of goods or services[9]Trademark lawyer cost
Utility patent: filing, search and examination$2,000 undiscounted; $800 small entity; $400 micro entity[9]Patent lawyer cost
Naturalization (Form N-400), paper filing$760[10]Immigration lawyer cost
Social Security disability representative fee (fee agreement)Capped at the lesser of 25% of past-due benefits or $9,200[11]SSDI lawyer cost

State court fees vary by state and often by county. Each state guide lists the filing fees we could verify on official sources.

What pushes a legal bill up

  • A contested opponent. Every motion, letter and hearing the other side forces is billable time.
  • Discovery volume. Collecting and reviewing documents, emails and records is often the largest block of hours in a lawsuit.
  • Experts and depositions. These add outside costs on top of lawyer time.
  • Urgency. Emergency filings and short deadlines compress work and leave less room to economize.
  • Disorganized information. Hours spent reconstructing a timeline from a shoebox of papers are billed at the same rate as legal analysis.
  • Scope creep. A flat fee covers what is written in the agreement; anything added later is usually billed separately.

When you may not need a full-service lawyer, and when you do

You may be able to handle a matter yourself, or with limited help, when the stakes are small and the process is designed for non-lawyers. California's small claims court, for example, handles claims up to $12,500 for individuals[12]; see small claims court cost. Many lawyers also offer limited scope (unbundled) help, where they handle only specific tasks such as reviewing a document or coaching you for a hearing[13].

Full representation is usually worth pricing when you face criminal charges, a lawsuit has been filed against you, significant property or custody is at stake, immigration status is involved, or the other side has a lawyer. In those situations, deadlines and procedural mistakes can cost more than the fee.

Ways to lower the cost

  • Get two or three written quotes for the same scope of work, and compare the total estimate, not just the hourly rate.
  • Use a state bar referral service. Several cap the first consultation, for example $25 or less for 30 minutes through the Illinois State Bar Association[14]. Details in our consultation fee guide.
  • Check legal aid eligibility. Programs funded by the Legal Services Corporation generally serve households at or below 125% of the poverty guidelines, which is $19,950 a year for one person in 2026[15]. See the legal aid guide and low-cost options.
  • Do the organizing yourself: a dated timeline, copies of key documents and a list of questions shorten every meeting.
  • Read every invoice. If you believe a bill is wrong, many state bars run fee dispute programs, such as California's Mandatory Fee Arbitration Program[16].

To run your own numbers, try the lawyer cost calculator.

faq.q: Will I pay $349 an hour for a lawyer?
faq.a: Not necessarily. $349 is Clio's national average across all practice areas and states for 2025. Rates vary with location, experience and type of case, so ask each lawyer for their rate in writing and for an estimate of total hours.

faq.q: Do lawyers charge for the first meeting?
faq.a: Some do and some do not. Contingency firms usually offer free intake, while other lawyers charge a flat or hourly consultation fee. State bar referral services in several states cap the first 30-minute consultation at a reduced fee.

faq.q: Can I negotiate a lawyer's fee?
faq.a: Often, yes. You can ask for a flat fee instead of hourly billing, a cap on hours for a defined stage, a lower rate for work done by junior staff, or limited-scope help with only part of the matter. Get any agreed change in writing.

faq.q: Are court filing fees included in a lawyer's quote?
faq.a: Usually not. Filing fees, service of process, transcripts and expert fees are normally billed as costs on top of the lawyer's fee. Ask the lawyer to list expected costs separately.

faq.q: What can I do if I think my lawyer overcharged me?
faq.a: Ask the lawyer for an itemized bill and an explanation first. If that does not resolve it, many state bars offer fee dispute or fee arbitration programs; your state guide lists the program we found for your state.
